title: Om

teacherSummary.text: Still aching for his son, Siddhartha sees his reflection resemble his own father and understands the circle of suffering. He confesses everything to Vasudeva, who leads him to listen; the river's voices—joy and sorrow, good and evil—blend into one word, Om. Siddhartha achieves serenity. Vasudeva, his work done, walks into the forest to die.

vocabulary.definition: The flower of a plant, or the essential organs of reproduction, with their appendages
vocabulary.context: Slowly blossomed, slowly ripened in Siddhartha the realisation, the knowledge, what wisdom actually was, what the goal of his long search was.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “blossom”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.definition: Having the power of serving or accomplishing fate
vocabulary.context: Was it not a comedy, a strange and stupid matter, this repetition, this running around in a fateful circle?
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “fateful”: -ful (Old English -full, "full of"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: A vessel for conveying passengers, merchandise, etc., across streams and other narrow waters
vocabulary.context: He no longer used the ferryboat, his eyes were starting to get weak, and not just his eyes; his arms and hands as well.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “ferryboat”: fer (Latin ferre, "to carry, bear"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.context: Slowly blossomed, slowly ripened in Siddhartha the realisation, the knowledge, what wisdom actually was, what the goal of his long search was.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “ripen”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.definition: To hinder from freedom of thought, speech, or action by something which impedes or confuses mental action
vocabulary.context: He reported everything, he was able to say everything, even the most embarrassing parts, everything could be said, everything shown, everything he could tell.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “embarrass”: em- (French en-/Latin in-, "into"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: The act of nourishing or nursing
vocabulary.context: But the wound still burned, longingly and bitterly Siddhartha thought of his son, nurtured his love and tenderness in his heart, allowed the pain to gnaw at him, committed all foolish acts of love.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “nurture”: -ure (Latin -ura, "act, result"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: One who, or that which, flees from danger, duty, restraint, etc.; a fugitive
vocabulary.context: He presented his wound, also told how he fled today, how he ferried across the water, a childish runaway, willing to walk to the city, how the river had laughed.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “runaway”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.context: It still resounded, full of suffering, searching, but other voices joined it, voices of joy and of suffering, good and bad voices, laughing and sad ones, a hundred voices, a thousand voices.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “resound”: re- (Latin re-, "back, again"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: Act of taking a bath or baths
vocabulary.context: To show his wound to this listener was the same as bathing it in the river, until it had cooled and become one with the river.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “bathing”: -ing (Old English -ing, action). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: The act of one who, or that which, weaves
vocabulary.context: Vasudeva was sitting in the hut and weaving a basket.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “weaving”: -ing (Old English -ing, action). Root not in our table: have students find it.

context.history: Hesse blends Hindu and Buddhist ideas of unity with Western mysticism.

significance: The climax: all opposites unite into one harmony, and the student becomes the master.
discussionQuestions: What does Siddhartha finally understand when he hears all the voices together?
Where does symbolism appear in this chapter, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this chapter connect to the book's larger concern with the search for self-knowledge?

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “Om,” how does Hesse show hearing the many voices? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the symbolism you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In Om, how does Hesse develop the idea of hearing the many voices? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the symbolism in the chapter helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Om develops the idea of hearing the many voices. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of symbolism and imagery shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of Om (where it begins, turns and ends) and its symbolism shape the reader's understanding of hearing the many voices. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what Om suggests about hearing the many voices. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the chapter's symbolism and imagery), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Hermann Hesse uses symbolism in Om to complicate the reader's understanding of hearing the many voices. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Om within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of hearing the many voices responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read Om alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the chapter's handling of hearing the many voices follows or bends those conventions, using the symbolism as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to Om and its treatment of hearing the many voices. State your method, show what it reveals in the chapter's symbolism and imagery, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads Om as evidence for a larger claim about hearing the many voices in Siddhartha. Connect close reading of the chapter to the whole novel, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Om as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of hearing the many voices. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Siddhartha.

satQuestions.passage: Slowly blossomed, slowly ripened in Siddhartha the realisation, the knowledge, what wisdom actually was, what the goal of his long search was. It was nothing but a readiness of the soul, an ability, a secret art, to think every moment, while living his life, the thought of oneness, to be able to feel and inhale the oneness. Slowly this blossomed in him, was shining back at him from Vasudeva’s old, childlike face: harmony, knowledge of the eternal perfection of the world, smiling, oneness.
satQuestions.prompt: Which choice best states a central concern of “Om”?
options: Injustice and the burden of silence
Obsession and the discovery of life

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: What does Siddhartha finally understand when he hears all the voices together? No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script: Today's words are blossomed, fateful, ferryboat, ripened, embarrassing. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check Webster's. Here is the first: “Slowly blossomed, slowly ripened in Siddhartha the realisation, the knowledge, what wisdom actually was, what the goal of his long search was.” Webster's says: The flower of a plant, or the essential organs of reproduction, with their appendages. Now the word history: “blossom”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin. “fateful”: -ful (Old English -full, "full of"). Root not in our table: have students find it. “ferryboat”: fer (Latin ferre, "to carry, bear"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary. Add each root to your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of Siddhartha would have known. Hesse blends Hindu and Buddhist ideas of unity with Western mysticism. Why does this chapter matter? The climax: all opposites unite into one harmony, and the student becomes the master. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for symbolism.
segments.script: Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. I read a sentence, stop, and ask what the author is doing. When I see symbolism, I underline it and write in the margin what effect it has. Here I notice the diction and the sentence rhythm, and I connect them to hearing the many voices.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Symbolism, Imagery, Theme.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of symbolism. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.
segments.passage: Slowly blossomed, slowly ripened in Siddhartha the realisation, the knowledge, what wisdom actually was, what the goal of his long search was. It was nothing but a readiness of the soul, an ability, a secret art, to think every moment, while living his life, the thought of oneness, to be able to feel and inhale the oneness. Slowly this blossomed in him, was shining back at him from Vasudeva’s old, childlike face: harmony, knowledge of the eternal perfection of the world, smiling, oneness.

segments.activity: Students annotate a new passage independently in the reader, then begin the writing prompt at their rigor.
segments.script: Your turn. Annotate the next page in the app for Symbolism, Imagery, Theme: at least three marks with a margin note each. Then open your writing prompt; your level is already set. Middle-school version: In “Om,” how does Hesse show hearing the many voices? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the symbolism you noticed as one piece of evidence. I will circulate and conference.

segments.activity: Structured discussion (think-pair-share or a short Socratic circle).
segments.script: Let's talk. Our question: How does this chapter connect to the search for self-knowledge? Every claim needs a page reference. Respond to the person before you by agreeing, extending or challenging with evidence.

segments.activity: Chapter quiz in the app, then a one-sentence exit ticket.
segments.script: Take the chapter quiz in the app. Then, in one sentence, tell me what this chapter suggests about hearing the many voices, backed by one short quotation.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
segments.script: Today we saw how symbolism shapes hearing the many voices. Tonight, read the next chapter and add two words to your etymology log.
